result.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers find the same core problems: a generic process diagram, vague research, an image dump and an empty learnings section. A is better because its fixes are concrete (claim then proof, before/after pairs with faults pinned to the old screen) and it never implies results; it marks every gap as a placeholder for the user to fill. B calls out the vague title more directly and lists senior-level signals well, but its example title suggests a cancellation-reduction result the user may not have, and its structure keeps a separate research section instead of tying each finding to the decision it drove. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers spot the same core problems: a generic process template, the vague 'users were frustrated' line, the backstory, the wireframe pile and the gallery with no explanation. B is better on what a skimming hiring reader needs to see first, and it builds its new order around 2–4 real decisions shown as claim-then-proof with before/after pairs. B also guards against made-up content: it labels its example as invented, says to include a decision only if it's real, and gives placeholders for the user to fill. A's example title assumes a cancellation result the user never mentioned.
